title: They weren’t asking for sin.
paragraphs:
They weren’t asking for sin.
They were asking for seats.
And that’s what makes it dangerous.

Because sometimes the most dangerous prayers don’t sound evil…
they sound spiritual.

“Lord, lift me.”
“Lord, use me.”
“Lord, bring me closer to You.”

But beneath those words…
there’s a quieter voice we don’t say out loud:

“Let me be seen.”
“Let me be first.”
“Let me matter more than the others.”

James and John walked with Jesus.
Saw miracles.
Heard truth straight from the mouth of God in flesh.
And still… they asked for power.
Read that again.

This isn’t a story about outsiders.
This is a warning to insiders.
People like us.

People who serve… but secretly compare.
People who obey… but quietly crave recognition.
People who look surrendered… but are still negotiating their position.
And maybe no one sees it.
But God does.

Because pride doesn’t always shout.
Sometimes it whispers in your prayers.

It hides in delayed obedience.
In silent competition.
In the subtle disappointment when someone else is chosen.
Let me ask you something—

When God blesses someone beside you…
do you celebrate?
Or does something tighten in your chest?
That tension?
That’s not hunger for God.
That’s hunger for position.
And that’s exactly where James and John were.

They said, “Let one sit at Your right and the other at Your left in Your glory” (Mark 10:37).
They wanted proximity without process.
Glory without the cross.
But Jesus answered them with a question that cuts deeper than any rebuke:
“Can you drink the cup I drink?” (Mark 10:38)

In other words—
Can you handle the suffering that comes before the seat?
Can you carry the cross before you carry influence?

Because in God’s kingdom…
position is not given to those who chase it.
It is entrusted to those who die to it.
AHA MOMENT:

The problem wasn’t that they wanted to be close to Jesus.
The problem was they wanted to be above others while doing it.
And that’s where many hearts are exposed.
SPIRITUAL MIRROR:

You don’t have to hate God to resist Him.
You just have to want His benefits more than His ways.
This is where it turns.

Jesus didn’t cancel them.
He didn’t replace them.
He didn’t expose them publicly to shame them.
He taught them.
He said, “Whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant” (Mark 10:43).
That flips everything.

Because the world says:
Climb higher.

Jesus says:
Bow lower.

The world says:
Be seen.

Jesus says:
Be surrendered.

The world says:
Take your seat.

Jesus says:
Pick up your cross.
And then He didn’t just say it—He lived it.
“The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45).
That’s the Gospel.

Not self-promotion.
Not platform-building.
Not spiritual branding.

A bleeding Savior.
A borrowed cross.
A holy ransom.
Because here’s the truth we don’t like to admit:
We didn’t just ask for seats.
We sinned.

We chose ourselves over God.
We built quiet kingdoms in our hearts.
We made life about us—even when we said it was about Him.
That’s sin.
And sin demands payment.
But Jesus stepped in.

He took the cup we couldn’t drink.
He carried the cross we couldn’t bear.
He died the death we deserved.
So we could receive the grace we never earned.
This is not about becoming a better version of yourself.

This is about dying to yourself…
and being raised with Christ.
Because salvation is not achieved by humility.
It is received through surrender to Jesus alone.
And here’s the conviction:

Some people want the language of surrender…
without the lifestyle of it.
That’s not Christianity.
That’s performance.
You are not called to be impressive.
You are called to be faithful.
You are not chosen because you are great.
You are made great because you belong to Christ.

And the moment you stop fighting for position…
is the moment God can trust you with purpose.
So what now?
Lay it down.

The comparison.
The hidden pride.
The need to be noticed.
Bring it to Jesus.

Not cleaned up.
Not justified.
Not explained.
Repent.

Turn from the throne you built in your heart
and bow before the King who died for it.
And here’s the hope—
Grace is not afraid of your ambition.
It redeems it.

Jesus can take your desire to be great…
and transform it into a life that actually matters.
Not in the eyes of people.
But in eternity.

If this is hitting deeper than you expected…
stay with it.
Not surface faith. Real transformation.
Because this isn’t about information.
It’s about formation.
And the next message?
It might expose the one thing you’ve been protecting.
